planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained, humus-rich epiphytic mix; wendlandii is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-12.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light to partial shade in a loose, fast-draining, bark-based aroid mix, and keep humidity elevated for the fullest rosette form. Unlike the familiar climbing philodendrons, Bird's Nest Philodendron is a self-heading, non-vining Costa Rican epiphyte that forms a tight, upright rosette of broad, paddle-shaped, thick, glossy dark-green leaves radiating outward like a shuttlecock or bird's nest. It stays compact for years, making it a good choice for shelves and tabletops where a sprawling climber would be unwelcome, and mature plants eventually produce basal offsets that can be divided and repotted. Let the mix dry slightly between waterings and avoid letting water sit in the crown.
sources: Marie Selby Botanical Gardens aroid collection notes

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained, humus-rich mix; plowmanii is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-12.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a coarse, well-drained, humus-rich mix, training the climbing stems onto a moss pole or trellis as the plant matures. Native to the Peru-Ecuador border region, Philodendron plowmanii produces large, heart-shaped leaves with a distinctive undulating, wavy margin and a mottled yellow-green to lime juvenile coloring that darkens toward a more uniform matte green with age, giving each plant an ever-changing look as it grows. It climbs at a slow to moderate pace and rewards consistent warmth and humidity with noticeably larger leaves. Let the top inch of mix dry between waterings and avoid cold drafts, which slow growth and can cause leaf spotting.
sources: Kew Gardens Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; grazielae is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-12.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, letting the thin trailing stems climb a small support or cascade from a hanging basket. Philodendron grazielae is a compact Brazilian climber with thin, glossy, simple heart-shaped leaves only a few inches long, giving it a finer, more delicate texture than most collector philodendrons and making it well suited to smaller totems, terrariums, and mixed-aroid displays. It is a fast, easy grower for a species-level philodendron and roots readily from stem cuttings with a node. Keep the mix evenly moist but not soggy and provide steady warmth and humidity for the densest foliage.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in a coarse, fast-draining, humus-rich mix; rugosum is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10b-12.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a coarse, fast-draining, humus-rich epiphytic mix, and let the mix dry slightly between waterings to avoid rot in this slow-growing species. Native to Ecuador's cloud forests, Philodendron rugosum earns its 'Pig Skin' nickname from its thick, leathery, dark-green leaves with a distinctly pebbled, rugose surface texture unlike the smooth or velvety foliage of most other collector philodendrons. Growth is slow and deliberate compared to faster climbing species, so give it steady warmth, elevated humidity, and patience rather than heavy fertilizing. Its cloud-forest origin makes it somewhat less heat-tolerant than lowland species, so protect it from prolonged temperatures above the mid-90s°F.
sources: Kew Gardens Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained, humus-rich mix; patriciae is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-12.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained, humus-rich mix, training the climbing stems onto a moss pole to encourage the largest, most richly colored leaves. Described from Ecuador in the past two decades, Philodendron patriciae produces broadly heart-shaped leaves with a soft, velvety sheen and pale, contrasting venation set against a deep olive-green surface, a texture and color combination that has made it a sought-after addition to shaded collector displays. It climbs steadily once established and benefits from consistently high humidity, which keeps the velvety leaf texture at its best and reduces the risk of crisping leaf edges. Water when the top inch of mix has dried and avoid cold, drafty locations.
sources: Kew Gardens Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant on a moss pole or piece of bark in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained, humus-rich mix; camposportoanum is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-12.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained, humus-rich mix, and give young plants a piece of bark or a mossy support to climb and shingle against. Native to the Amazon basin of Brazil, Guyana, and Venezuela, Philodendron camposportoanum shows one of the most dramatic juvenile-to-adult leaf transformations in the genus: small, simple, glossy ovate leaves on young plants give way to larger, deeply three-lobed leaves with pronounced side lobes once the plant matures and begins climbing in good light. Bright, filtered light encourages the transition to the more dramatic lobed adult foliage, while lower light keeps growth in the smaller juvenile form longer. Let the mix dry slightly between waterings and maintain warm, humid conditions typical of lowland tropical understories.
